en: The Text on the Precepts for Leaving [Worldly Life] for Śrāmaṇerikās; from the *Śrāmaṇerikā-śīla-sūtra*, translated during the Eastern Jin Dynasty (translator lost).
A virtuous woman named [Name] says: This foul and evil body received by me belongs to the ranks of the lowly and debased.
Unable to continue his lowly practice,
he reproached himself with remorse and wished to become a disciple, vowing to receive and uphold the true precepts and practice them throughout his life.
For what reason did he become a śrāmaṇera?
Because one has taken refuge in the Buddha, taken refuge in the Dharma, and taken refuge in the Saṅgha of bhikṣus;
because one has shaved the head and donned the kāṣāya—
how many precepts are there?
A śrāmaṇera has ten precepts:
First, for as long as life lasts, one must not kill living beings, nor must one teach others to kill.
Second, for as long as life lasts, one must not steal, nor must one teach others to steal.
3. For as long as life lasts, one must not engage in sexual misconduct, nor must one teach others to engage in sexual misconduct.
4. For as long as life lasts, one must not marry, nor must one teach others to marry.
5. For as long as life lasts, one must not speak falsely, nor should one teach others to speak falsely.
6. For as long as life lasts, one must not sing or dance, nor should one teach others to sing or dance, nor should one play the zither or blow the flute.
7. For as long as life lasts, one must not wear perfumes, flowers, unguents, or powders, nor should one instruct others to apply such unguents and powders.
8. For as long as life lasts, one must not lie upon high or ornate beds carved with engravings, nor should one instruct others to make such fine beds for lying upon.
9. For as long as life lasts, one must not drink alcohol, nor should one teach others to drink alcohol.
10. For as long as life lasts, one must not eat again after midday has passed, nor should one teach others to eat [at such times].
Regarding the seventy matters of dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*):
one must not wear garments of silk or brocade; one must not give such dyed garments to others;
one must not engage in malicious speech or flirtatious banter; and one must not teach others to speak of trivial or unnecessary matters.
One must not look at one's own body with a laywoman (upāsikā) and laugh loudly.
One must not expose one's body in a secluded place to fondle it.
One must not look into a mirror, rub or wipe the face, or paint the eyebrows.
One must not speak with words of anger, resentment, shame, or malice.
One must not harbor thoughts of engaging in sexual intercourse with men or inquire about such matters regarding an upāsikā.
One must not sit upon a seat made of wool or cotton.
One must not wear boots or shoes, nor should one make them.
One must not covet household wealth or forcibly demand goods from others.
One must not sit upon the beds of other women’s families, inspect their utensils, or look at their clothes, remarking that these are beautiful while those are ugly.
Those aged sixteen and above should become *śrāmaṇeras*.
Being naturally free from blemish, chaste, virtuous, and complete in their integrity without any defilement or disgrace, they may enter the Way only if their parents grant them permission.
One who has never been chaste and virtuous should not practice the Way.
One who conceals illnesses like a stone statue should not practice the Way.
Such a person must not sleep in the same room as the community of bhikṣus.
One must not sit together with them.
One must not mock one another.
One must not lie down within the robes and bedding of a śrāmaṇera.
One must not confuse dharma-robes with common utensils, nor mistakenly wear monastic robes.
One must not hand objects directly to a man;
if one wishes to give something, one should place it on the ground and have him pick it up.
One must not bathe in the open with an upāsikā.
One must not go alone to a monastic dwelling to inquire about the meaning of the Dharma.
One must not speak of worldly matters.
One must not laugh at the words of the sutras;
one must not look left or right;
one must not rest one's hands upon the table.
There are five matters regarding the reception of the scriptures:
one should walk together with an elder nun;
one should sit six chi away [from her].
Kneel with your right knee on the ground; you may ask about the meaning,
but you must recognize the phrasing and punctuation.
There are four matters for visiting a teacher who is ill; there are those who should visit out of kinship:
three people traveling together, and one within six feet of the bed.
Having prostrated with the right knee on the ground and finished the inquiry after speaking, one should depart; one must not discuss matters [of business].
There are five matters regarding lying down at night:
one should place one's head toward the direction of the Buddha.
One should lie down in a hunched position without stretching out one's legs;
one must not lie on one's back yawning repeatedly;
and one must not expose oneself by baring the body.
One must not let one's hands come near impure places.
When visiting the house of a donor (dānapati), there are five matters to attend to:
one should first go to the monastery (vihāra) to pay homage to the Buddha.
Next, pay homage to the preceptor and the monks;
only when invited by a laywoman (upāsikā) should one enter;
one must then inform the preceptor and the monks.
One should gaze straight ahead at a distance of six feet while sitting alone upon the couch.
When staying in the house of a donor (*dānapati*), there are five things that are contrary to the Dharma:
one must not enter the women’s quarters to engage in idle chatter or play.
One must not sit and eat beneath the hearth;
one must not engage in private conversation with female servants;
one must not go alone behind the house, nor enter the latrine together with another person.
One must not enter the men’s latrines.
There are five matters regarding entering the bathhouse:
one must not wash together with a female lay follower (upāsikā).
One must not wash together with maidservants;
one must not wash together with small children;
one must not take water that has already been used by others.
One must not look at one's own private parts.
There are five matters regarding the burning of incense:
one must not look far off to the left or right.
One must not burn incense alone with an upāsaka;
one must not be alone with a female servant;
nor should one drag one's feet.
One must not turn one's back toward an image.
Upon rising in the morning, there are five matters to attend to:
first, one should purify oneself and then put on the dharma robes.
First, pay homage to the scriptures and images;
next, pay homage to the preceptor and the monks;
then, step back six feet to offer greetings.
He then stepped back and went out the door.
When the Master converses with him, there are five matters:
if he asks about the meaning of the sutras or the precepts and does not know it, he should request instruction.
If one is reprimanded, one should immediately repent of one's transgression;
one must not conceal it,
nor must one attempt to justify oneself.
One must not look upon the teacher with an evil eye.
There are four matters regarding the washing of robes:
one should do so in a secluded place and remain in a long-kneeling posture.
One should discard foul water in a secluded place, not upon a public path;
one should wait for it to dry before collecting it,
and must not allow it to fall upon the ground.
There are five matters regarding traveling on a journey:
one should travel together with three persons;
one should travel together with a mahābhikṣuṇī.
If one is to walk together with an upāsikā,
one should keep one's gaze fixed six feet ahead and wear the dharma robes.
The Master said:
"By nature, women tend to manifest various eccentricities and postures; they delight in lewdness and lack of propriety, which is why they are called 'women.

Now, through self-awakening, they have received the great grace of Śākyamuni Buddha, who has opened the path for them throughout the three realms. Yet, those who recognize their own fundamental conduct and take refuge in the Buddha are few."
The Buddha said:
"Observe the human realm, from the twenty-eight heavens above down to the eighteen hells below; all are suffering and devoid of joy.
Therefore, he established the precepts to instruct future generations.
The Buddha told his disciples:
"To pursue the Way is exceedingly difficult; few are able to leave home and sever the six sense-faculties.
To receive the Buddha’s grave precepts and renounce all craving and desire—those who can do so are rare."
The Buddha told his disciples:
"Be careful not to recklessly ordain the śrāmaṇera Li.
A woman’s demeanor is difficult to keep pleasing; in an instant, she may again give rise to evil intentions."
For example, water bubbles arise and perish one after another, having no permanence or stability.
One who can perceive the faculties of others and observe their great conduct, seeing that their past offenses have now been exhausted and they are ready to attain the Way, must quickly deliver them.
"Unless one is a Bodhisattva or an Arhat, one may not ordain a bhikṣuṇī.
With the exception of the procedures for visiting [the preceptor] and reciting the *Poṣadha* (precept-recitation),
the *Karmadāna* (Venerable of Affairs) must first prepare the *śalākā* voting sticks, incense, lamps, and the text of the precepts.

Having thoroughly swept and cleaned the vihāra, he struck the *gandī* bell; after burning incense, prostrating before the Buddha, and completing the chanting of dhāraṇīs and prayers, he offered prayers for the Mother of Demons (*Hārītī*).
Each then took their seat, adjusted their dharma robes, joined their palms, and remained in silent stillness.
The *vina* then dispatches the incense-bearer attendants,
each of whom recites a verse.
The *vina* stands inside the door and chants three times:
"Once the laypeople have departed and the *poṣadha* ceremony for visiting [the assembly] is concluded," he says.
He snaps his fingers three times to send the laypeople far away so that they do not hear the recitation of the precepts (*śīla*).
When the sound has ceased, he opens the door, and the *karmadāna* (Venerable) proclaims:
"Sit in meditation, set aside visitors, and remain silent; today is the Poṣadha.
Having recited this three times, the *karmadāna* (Vina) takes up the counting sticks (*śalākā*).

He kneels before the senior nun (*sthavirī*), and as each person participating in the Poṣadha gives him a stick, he likewise takes them for himself. He then returns to collect the sticks and places them separately in another spot.
He then takes back the uncounted voting sticks (*śalākā*), holds them in his hand, and asks before the senior nun:
"Who has not received a stick?
Those who have not yet received one should say 'not'; those who have already received one should remain silent."
When this was finished, the *karmadāna* counted the tally-sticks to determine how many people were present and their respective numbers.
The *karmadāna* then announced:

"With the exception of so-and-so and such-and-such persons, according to the year and month—saying 'the fifteenth' when it is the fifteenth, and 'the thirtieth' when the month ends—we shall recite the precepts within the monastery of the donor from such-and-such state, such-and-such commandery, and such-and-such district."

By the merit of upholding and reciting the precepts, may it flow back to the great donors and their kin and dependents, so that all may be peaceful and secure; for those who have passed away, may they be reborn among gods and humans to increase their merit; and may all those in distress throughout the ten directions be universally liberated.

When each had finished reciting the benediction, the *karmadāna* knelt before the senior nun and requested the person capable of reciting the precepts to do so; he further requested another person to perform three *bhāṣya* chants and read from the scriptures.

When the recitation of the scripture is finished, there is a chant; once the chant is concluded, the elder (upādhyāya) offers a general prayer of blessing, while the nuns of the lower seats all kneel prostrate to receive the blessing.
The *karmadāna* then calls out:
"Everyone, together pay homage to the Buddha."
After the *prajñāpāramitā* has been venerated, the nuns seated below all pay homage to the senior nuns (*mahābhikṣuṇī*). Then, the *karmadāna* kneels and proclaims:
"Be seated as you please.
He then invites the person who will recite the precepts and the person who will read the scriptures to sit together on a single couch.

Regarding the *Śrāmaṇerī-vinaya-vibhaṅga*: according to the title of this precept, the National Edition (Guoben), the Song Edition, and the *Kaiyuan lu* all refer to it as the *Śrāmaṇerī-vinaya-vibhaṅga*.
The Dan edition simply calls this "The Text on Miscellaneous Precepts for Śrāmaṇerikās.
However, upon examining the correct version, none of these editions are accurate. Why is this so?
Regarding the character "li" (離) in this translation and the character "ni" (尼) in other translations, they differ merely in their Sanskrit pronunciation—like the dialectal variations of Chu and Xia.
This is neither the text for the *pārājika* precepts of a śrāmaṇerikā nor the text for the miscellaneous (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*) precepts of a śrāmaṇerikā.
Furthermore, this deviates from the original text; therefore, it would now be correct to simply title it "The Text on the Ordination of Śrāmaṇeras.
However, as there is no authoritative basis for this, I do not dare to make such a correction immediately.
I have recorded these thoughts as they are, awaiting those gentlemen who appreciate antiquity and value elegance and correctness.
